papers.title: Trading Before a Committed Rebalance
papers.abstract: An institution must complete a portfolio adjustment, but traders who prepare inventory for it can choose whether to participate. We study how public forecasts affect the institution's cost in a Bayesian execution game with optional activation, transient impact, and uniform-price terminal completion. The curvature of equilibrium cost as a function of the posterior target mean determines the value of information. In the scalar model, information benefits every fixed participation roster. Optional supply can reverse this ranking at entry, at full participation, and in a smooth interior with lognormal activation costs. For centered scalar targets, information weakly lowers cost relative to no information, strictly when the posterior mean is nonzero with positive probability. Centered Gaussian precision gains are always beneficial. An exact symmetric finite-population equilibrium identifies how information resolution and individual strategic size interact near entry. A portfolio extension gives a matrix criterion for the fixed-roster ranking, which can fail under general cross-impact. Even with isotropic execution, shared activation allows equally accurate signals about target magnitude and composition to have opposite execution values under one unchanged prior. Intraday ETF price data is used to characterize target uncertainty and trading conditions without identifying activation or institutional costs.

papers.title: Shared Models, Selective Trading, and Order Flow
papers.abstract: We study whether the diversity of language models installed in a trading population carries over to the orders that reach the market. In simulated markets with five agents from each of three open-weight model families, we change only how a corporate announcement is presented and estimate each family's share of active orders. In two matched experiments, explanatory layoff text multiplies Mistral's participation by 5.3 (from 14.0% to 74.7% of opportunities) and raises its share of announcement-round orders from 17.5% to 57.4%. In a preregistered study of six new events, adding one favorable and one unfavorable evaluation to identical facts changes active composition in a main sample and in an independently worded replication (average e-values of 6.3x10^25 and 6.7x10^40, against a threshold of 20). Within an event, the change reallocates on average 21% of active decisions across families in the main sample and 14% in the replication. The same reallocation appears under both wordings in three of the six events; in the other three, the families that gain differ. Evaluative text also lowers every family's average participation and lowers executed net flow in all twelve event-sample cells, and family contributions mostly reinforce one another. In the financing event of the first study, active composition changed substantially while net flow barely moved, because family responses offset one another. In a stylized market-clearing benchmark, price accuracy depends on both the number and the composition of active traders. The experiments do not identify why the models respond to evaluations, and they do not estimate effects on price accuracy.

papers.title: Neural Estimation of Irreversibility in Real and Simulated Limit Order Book Paths
papers.abstract: A path indistinguishable from its own reverse carries no arrow of time, so time irreversibility is a necessary condition for a directed mechanism to be readable from trajectories alone. In finance it has been measured only on scalar series such as returns and volatility. We define the irreversibility rate of a coarse-grained limit order book path as the forward-to-reverse log-density ratio per event, and estimate it from three weeks of Nasdaq market-by-order data with an order-invariant MLP and a temporal convolutional network that receive identical blocks. For NVDA, the order-invariant and order-sensitive estimates are 0.036 and 0.054 nats per event, respectively. Their difference, the ordering increment, is 0.018. A surrogate preserving the coarse one-step transition table recovers 30 percent less irreversibility than the observed paths. The increment is positive for all twelve symbols on every held-out daytime date, and for NVDA in each session window. Across the twelve symbols, its share of the ordered rate increases roughly logarithmically with the spread in ticks. The increment changes more than tenfold with the coarse-graining scale. Neither a linear score nor any single feature group reproduces the full fitted rate. A queue-reactive simulator calibrated on the same days matches the market's ordered rate, 0.052 against 0.054, yet its ordering increment is 0.0006 against 0.018, building temporal asymmetry out of block composition instead of block order. We propose the ordering and scale profile of path irreversibility as a benchmark for order book simulators. Code and audit materials are available at https://github.com/hjyeo30/lob-irreversibility.
